questions.q: Which decimal is equal to the fraction 609/10000?
questions.a: 0.0609: the denominator 10000 has four zeroes, so 609 ÷ 10000 moves the point four places left, giving 0.0609.

questions.q: Jonali buys 40 g of cloves at a spice shop. Since 1 kg = 1000 g, the weight of the cloves in kilograms is
(a) Write the fraction 207/1000 as a sum of one-tenths, one-hundredths and one-thousandths. (b) Write it as a decimal.
s: Writes the decimal 0.207, with 0 in the hundredths place

questions.q: Use the rule of moving the decimal point to find: (a) 56 ÷ 100 (b) 4.7 ÷ 1000 (c) 0.38 × 100
questions.a: (a) Two places left: 56 ÷ 100 = 0.56. (b) Three places left, adding zeroes in front: 4.7 ÷ 1000 = 0.0047. (c) Two places right: 0.38 × 100 = 38.

questions.q: Match each calculation in Column I with its value in Column II. Column I: 1. 9.6 ÷ 100  2. 0.96 × 1000  3. 96 ÷ 10000  4. 0.0096 × 1000. Column II: a. 9.6  b. 0.096  c. 960  d. 0.0096
True or False: When 2.5 litres of lassi is poured equally into 100 small cups, each cup gets 0.25 litre.
questions.a: False. Each cup gets 2.5 ÷ 100 = 0.025 litre (the point moves two places left), which is 25 mL; 0.25 litre would be 250 mL.

questions.q: Consider the following statements. Statement I: 3.06 ÷ 100 = 0.0306. Statement II: 70 ÷ 1000 = 0.7. Statement III: 0.45 × 1000 = 450. Which of the statements are true?
questions.a: Only I and III: 3.06 ÷ 100 = 0.0306 and 0.45 × 1000 = 450. Statement II is false because 70 ÷ 1000 = 0.07.

questions.q: A jeweller in Jaipur weighs a small gold ring on a balance that shows grams with three digits after the decimal point. The display reads 4.375 g. She is making a set of identical rings for a wedding order, and she writes every weight first in grams and then, for the bill, in kilograms (1 kg = 1000 g). (a) Write 4.375 as ones + tenths + hundredths + thousandths. (b) Write 4.375 as one fraction with denominator 1000. (c) Find the weight of 10 such rings. (d) Find the weight of 100 such rings in grams and then in kilograms.

A grocery shop in Nagpur sells the same cumin seeds in three packs: a 10 g sachet for ₹4.20, a 100 g packet for ₹38.50 and a 1 kg pack for ₹365. (a) Find the cost of 1 kg if it is bought as 100 g packets. (b) Find the cost of 1 kg if it is bought as 10 g sachets. (c) Find the price of 1 g of cumin in each of the three packs. (d) Which pack is the cheapest per gram? (e) How much more does a buyer pay for 1 kg in sachets than for the 1 kg pack?
questions.a: (a) 10 packets make 1 kg: 38.50 × 10 = ₹385. (b) 100 sachets make 1 kg: 4.20 × 100 = ₹420. (c) Sachet 4.20 ÷ 10 = ₹0.42, packet 38.50 ÷ 100 = ₹0.385, 1 kg pack 365 ÷ 1000 = ₹0.365 per gram. (d) The 1 kg pack, at ₹0.365 per gram. (e) 420 - 365 = ₹55 more.
s: Part (d): the 1 kg pack is cheapest per gram

questions.q: One notebook costs ₹18.5. How much do 4 such notebooks cost?
Using the rule for multiplying decimals, how many digits after the decimal point does the product 3.4 × 0.27 have?
questions.a: 3: 3.4 has 1 digit and 0.27 has 2 digits after the point, so the product 34 × 27 = 918 gets 1 + 2 = 3 places, giving 0.918.

questions.q: State the rule for placing the decimal point in the product of two decimals. Use it to find 0.6 × 0.3.
questions.a: Remove the decimal points and multiply; the product has as many digits after the point as the two numbers have together. 6 × 3 = 18 and 1 + 1 = 2 places, so 0.6 × 0.3 = 0.18.
s: States the rule: total number of decimal places of the two numbers

questions.q: (a) Write 1.2 and 0.7 as fractions with denominator 10. (b) Multiply the fractions to find 1.2 × 0.7 as a decimal.
Find the products: (a) 7 × 0.4 (b) 2.5 × 1.2 (c) 0.15 × 0.3
questions.a: (a) 7 × 4 = 28 with 1 decimal place: 2.8. (b) 25 × 12 = 300 with 2 places: 3.00 = 3. (c) 15 × 3 = 45 with 3 places: 0.045.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 1.6 × 1.25 = 2, so the product of two decimals can be a counting number. Reason (R): The product of two decimals can never be a counting number.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: 16 × 125 = 2000 with 3 decimal places gives 2.000 = 2, a counting number, so R's claim that this can never happen is wrong.

questions.q: A farmer in Nashik puts a fence of 3 rounds of wire around a rectangular garden 12.5 m long and 8.75 m wide. The wire costs ₹18.40 per metre. (a) Find the total length of wire needed. (b) Find the cost of the wire.

The Rao family in Vijayawada buys milk at ₹56.40 per litre. In June (30 days) they buy 1.5 litres every day, and in July (31 days) they buy 2.25 litres every day. (a) Find the cost of milk for one day in June. (b) Find the bill for the whole of June. (c) Find the cost of milk for one day in July. (d) Find the bill for the whole of July. (e) The family has set aside ₹3900 for July's milk. Is this enough? If not, how much more do they need?

Mrs Iyer needs 12.5 kg of rice for the month. Shop P sells loose rice at ₹62.40 per kg. Shop Q sells 5 kg bags at ₹298.75 a bag, and loose rice at ₹64.80 per kg. At Shop Q she would buy two bags and 2.5 kg loose. Find the cost at each shop and decide where she should buy, and how much she saves.
questions.a: Shop P: 12.5 × 62.40 = ₹780. Shop Q: two bags cost 2 × 298.75 = ₹597.50 and 2.5 kg loose costs 2.5 × 64.80 = ₹162, so ₹759.50 in all. She should buy at Shop Q and saves 780 - 759.50 = ₹20.50.
s: Loose rice at Shop Q: ₹162, total ₹759.50

questions.q: In which of these multiplications is the product less than both the numbers multiplied?
questions.a: 0.6 × 0.9: both numbers lie between 0 and 1, so the product 0.54 is less than both.

questions.q: Given that 23 × 17 = 391, the value of 2.3 × 1.7 is
questions.a: 3.91: the two numbers have 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places together, so the point goes two places from the right of 391.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The product 1.6 × 2.5 is greater than both 1.6 and 2.5. Reason (R): When both numbers are greater than 1, their product is greater than both numbers.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: 1.6 × 2.5 = 4, which is greater than both, as must happen when both numbers are greater than 1.

questions.q: True or False: The product 0.5 × 12 is less than 12 but greater than 0.5.
questions.a: True. 0.5 × 12 = 6. One number lies between 0 and 1 and the other is greater than 1, so the product lies between them: 0.5 < 6 < 12.
s: Finds the product 6 and shows it lies between 0.5 and 12

questions.q: Consider the following statements. Statement I: 0.9 × 0.9 is less than 0.9. Statement II: 1.1 × 0.95 is greater than 1.1. Statement III: 4.2 × 0.5 lies between 0.5 and 4.2. Which of the statements are true?
questions.a: Only I and III: 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81 is less than 0.9, and 4.2 × 0.5 = 2.1 lies between 0.5 and 4.2. Statement II is false because multiplying 1.1 by 0.95, a number less than 1, gives 1.045, which is less than 1.1.

questions.q: Given that 45 × 32 = 1440, write down without multiplying again: (a) 4.5 × 3.2 (b) 0.45 × 0.032 (c) 450 × 0.32
Ravi says, "Multiplying always makes a number bigger, so 64 × 0.75 must be more than 64." Do you agree? Find the product and explain.
questions.a: No. 64 × 0.75 = 48, which is less than 64. Multiplying by a number between 0 and 1, such as 0.75, takes only a part of 64, so the product is less than 64 (though greater than 0.75). Ravi's idea holds only when multiplying by a number greater than 1.
s: Explains that multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 gives a smaller product

questions.q: Neha has four number cards: 0.6, 0.75, 1.2 and 2.5. She picks two different cards and multiplies them. (a) Which pair gives a product less than both cards? Find that product. (b) Which pair gives a product greater than both cards? Find that product. (c) Find 0.75 × 2.5 and say where it lies compared with its two cards. (d) Neha claims that every pair that includes 0.6 gives a product less than 1. Check her claim.
questions.a: (a) Only 0.6 and 0.75 are both between 0 and 1: 0.6 × 0.75 = 0.45, less than both. (b) Only 1.2 and 2.5 are both greater than 1: 1.2 × 2.5 = 3, greater than both. (c) 0.75 × 2.5 = 1.875, which lies between 0.75 and 2.5. (d) 0.6 × 0.75 = 0.45 and 0.6 × 1.2 = 0.72, but 0.6 × 2.5 = 1.5, which is more than 1, so the claim is false.
s: Part (d): checks all three pairs and rejects the claim since 0.6 × 2.5 = 1.5

questions.q: Making the denominator 100, the fraction 7/4 written as a decimal is
Rohan divides 9.5 by 4 using long division (division using place value). When must he put the decimal point in the quotient?
o: When he moves from dividing the Ones to dividing the Tenths
Never, because 9.5 ÷ 4 has no decimal part
questions.a: When he moves from dividing the Ones to dividing the Tenths: the quotient's digits after that point are tenths, hundredths and so on, giving 9.5 ÷ 4 = 2.375.

questions.q: A carpenter cuts a 6.4 m long pipe into 8 equal pieces. The length of each piece, in centimetres, is
(a) By what number should you multiply the numerator and denominator of 13/8 to get the denominator 1000? (b) Hence write 13/8 as a decimal.
Use long division to find: (a) 87 ÷ 2 (b) 87 ÷ 4 (c) 87 ÷ 8 (d) 8.7 ÷ 4. (e) In (c), how many times did you regroup a remainder into Tenths, Hundredths or Thousandths before the remainder became 0?
questions.a: (a) 43.5 (b) 21.75 (c) 10.875 (d) 2.175. (e) Three times: 7 Ones were regrouped as 70 Tenths (remainder 6), 6 Tenths as 60 Hundredths (remainder 4) and 4 Hundredths as 40 Thousandths (remainder 0), so the quotient has three decimal places.
s: Part (e): three regroupings, into tenths, hundredths and thousandths

questions.q: True or False: 0.09 ÷ 6 = 0.015.
questions.a: True. 0 Ones and 0 Tenths give 0.0; 9 Hundredths ÷ 6 = 1 Hundredth with 3 Hundredths left; regroup 3 Hundredths as 30 Thousandths, and 30 ÷ 6 = 5 Thousandths. So 0.09 ÷ 6 = 0.015 (check: 0.015 × 6 = 0.09).

questions.q: Assertion (A): 17 ÷ 4 = 4.25. Reason (R): 4 is a factor of 100, so 17/4 can be written as 425/100.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: since 4 × 25 = 100, 17/4 = (17 × 25)/100 = 425/100 = 4.25.

questions.q: Dinesh divides 5.6 kg of dal equally into 8 packets and writes, "Each packet holds 7 kg, because 56 ÷ 8 = 7." Show that he must be wrong, find the correct amount, and say where he lost the decimal point.
questions.a: Each packet cannot hold more than the 5.6 kg he started with, so 7 kg is impossible. 5 Ones ÷ 8 = 0 Ones; regroup as 56 Tenths, and 56 Tenths ÷ 8 = 7 Tenths, so each packet holds 0.7 kg. He divided 56 as if it were Ones, forgetting that 56 here means 56 Tenths.
s: Shows 7 kg is impossible (more than the total)
Explains that 56 is 56 Tenths, not 56 Ones

questions.q: The eco-club of a school in Bhubaneswar has 8 members. In one week of 5 school days they collected 37 kg of waste paper and sold it to a recycler at ₹14 per kg. The money is shared equally among the 8 members for their club diaries. For next week, the club wants each member to get at least ₹80. Their plan is that each member brings 1.25 kg of paper every school day, sold at the same rate. (a) How much money did the club get this week? (b) How much does each member get? (c) What was the average amount of paper collected per school day? (d) Will next week's plan give each member at least ₹80? Show your working.
questions.a: (a) 37 × 14 = ₹518. (b) 518 ÷ 8 = ₹64.75 each. (c) 37 ÷ 5 = 7.4 kg per day. (d) Paper next week: 8 × 1.25 × 5 = 50 kg; money: 50 × 14 = ₹700; each member: 700 ÷ 8 = ₹87.50, which is more than ₹80, so yes, the plan works.

questions.q: The value of 36 ÷ 0.4 is
questions.a: 90: multiply both numbers by 10 to get 360 ÷ 4 = 90.

questions.q: To find 7.25 ÷ 0.25, we make the divisor a counting number. Which division has the same quotient as 7.25 ÷ 0.25?
questions.a: 725 ÷ 25: multiplying both the dividend and the divisor by 100 keeps the quotient the same, and 725 ÷ 25 = 29.

questions.q: (a) Multiply both 2.88 and 0.12 by 100 and write the new division. (b) Find 2.88 ÷ 0.12.
True or False: When a number is divided by 0.5, the quotient is always smaller than the number.
questions.a: False. Dividing by a number between 0 and 1 gives a quotient greater than the dividend. For example, 8 ÷ 0.5 = 80 ÷ 5 = 16, which is greater than 8.

questions.q: Match each division in Column I with its quotient in Column II. Column I: 1. 4.8 ÷ 0.06  2. 0.48 ÷ 6  3. 4.8 ÷ 0.6  4. 0.48 ÷ 0.6. Column II: a. 0.8  b. 80  c. 0.08  d. 8
Assertion (A): 2.4 ÷ 0.8 = 3. Reason (R): Dividing by any decimal always gives a quotient greater than the dividend.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: 2.4 ÷ 0.8 = 24 ÷ 8 = 3. But a decimal divisor greater than 1 gives a smaller quotient, for example 2.4 ÷ 1.2 = 2, which is less than 2.4.

questions.q: A juice stall in Nashik has 6.3 litres of sugarcane juice. It pours the juice into glasses holding 0.35 litre each and sells each glass for ₹15. (a) How many glasses can it fill? (b) How much money does it get by selling all of them?

A farmer in Karnal can hire one of two tractors to plough an 18-acre field. Tractor A ploughed 5.4 acres in 1.5 hours and Tractor B ploughed 7.2 acres in 2.4 hours. Tractor A costs ₹412.50 for each hour and Tractor B costs ₹337.80 for each hour. (a) Find the acres each tractor ploughs in 1 hour. (b) Which tractor is faster? (c) How many hours does each tractor need for the 18-acre field? (d) Find the hire cost of each tractor for the field. (e) The farmer wants the cheaper choice. Which tractor should he hire, and how much does he save?
Which of these divisions never ends when worked out as a decimal?
questions.a: 2 ÷ 3: the remainder 2 comes back at every step, so it goes on as 0.666... The others end: 0.75, 0.875 and 1.8.

questions.q: In the long division of 10 by 3, what remainder do we get at every step?
questions.a: 1: each time 10 of a place is divided by 3, we get 3 with 1 left over, so the division never ends and 10 ÷ 3 = 3.333...

questions.q: (a) Divide 1 by 3 and write the first four digits after the decimal point. (b) Will this division ever end? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 1 ÷ 3 = 0.3333... (b) No. At every step the remainder is 1, so the same step (10 ÷ 3 = 3, remainder 1) repeats for ever.
s: Part (b): No, because the remainder 1 keeps repeating

questions.q: Assertion (A): The division 5 ÷ 11 never ends. Reason (R): In the long division of 5 by 11, the remainders go 5, 6, 5, 6, ..., so a remainder repeats and the remainder is never 0.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: once the remainder 5 returns, the same steps repeat for ever, giving 5 ÷ 11 = 0.4545...

questions.q: True or False: The division 1 ÷ 6 never ends.
questions.a: True. 10 tenths ÷ 6 = 1 tenth, remainder 4; then 40 ÷ 6 = 6, remainder 4 again, and again at every step. The remainder 4 repeats, so 1 ÷ 6 = 0.1666... never ends.

questions.q: (a) Divide 4 by 7 by long division and write the first six digits after the decimal point, with the remainder after each digit. (b) Without dividing further, write the 7th and 8th digits after the point and explain how you know.
questions.a: (a) 4 ÷ 7 = 0.571428...: the digits 5, 7, 1, 4, 2, 8 leave remainders 5, 1, 3, 2, 6, 4. (b) After the sixth digit the remainder is 4 again, which is where we started, so the same steps repeat: the 7th digit is 5 and the 8th is 7.
s: Part (b): 7th digit 5 and 8th digit 7, because the remainder 4 has returned

questions.q: (a) Find 10 ÷ 9 to four digits after the point and state the remainder at each step. (b) Find 7 ÷ 12 to four digits after the point and state the remainders. (c) Find 25 ÷ 8 and say whether it ends. (d) When we divide by 12, how many different non-zero remainders are possible? (e) Using (b) and (d), explain why the digits of 7 ÷ 12 must go on repeating for ever.
questions.a: (a) 10 ÷ 9 = 1.1111..., with remainder 1 at every step. (b) 7 ÷ 12 = 0.5833..., the remainders go 10, 4, 4, 4, ... (c) 25 ÷ 8 = 3.125; the remainder becomes 0, so it ends. (d) Eleven: 1, 2, 3, ..., 11. (e) In (b) the remainder is never 0, and by (d) there are only 11 possible non-zero remainders, so a remainder must come back; here 4 comes back at the very next step, so the same step repeats and the digit 3 repeats for ever.
s: Part (e): only 11 remainders and none is 0, so one returns (4) and the digit 3 repeats

questions.q: A tailor in Kanpur has a 7 m length of cloth for cushion covers, all of the same length. Her measuring tape is marked only in centimetres and millimetres, so she wants each length to be an exact number of millimetres with no cloth wasted. She is deciding between 6 cushion covers and 8 cushion covers. (a) Find 7 ÷ 6 as a decimal to four digits after the point. (b) Does 7 ÷ 6 end? Give a reason. (c) If she cuts each of the 6 pieces as 1.16 m, how much cloth is left over, in centimetres? (d) Find 7 ÷ 8 and decide which choice, 6 or 8 covers, lets her use all the cloth with exact cuts on her tape.
questions.a: (a) 7 ÷ 6 = 1.1666... (b) No: after the first step the remainder 4 repeats at every step, so the 6s go on for ever. (c) 6 × 1.16 = 6.96 m is used, so 7 - 6.96 = 0.04 m = 4 cm is left over. (d) 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875 m = 875 mm, which ends and can be marked exactly; so 8 covers lets her use all the cloth, while 6 covers cannot.
s: Part (b): never ends, because the remainder 4 repeats
Part (d): 0.875 m = 875 mm, so she should choose 8 covers

questions.q: How many days does the Earth take to go once around the Sun?
questions.a: 365.2422 days: a calendar year of 365 days is 0.2422 day short of one full revolution.

questions.q: Under the final leap-year rule, which of these years is a leap year?
questions.a: 2400: it is a century year, but it is divisible by 400, so it is a leap year. 2100, 1900 and 2200 are century years not divisible by 400.

questions.q: State the final rule that decides whether a year is a leap year. Use it to say whether the year 2028 is a leap year.
questions.a: A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except a year divisible by 100, which is a leap year only if it is also divisible by 400. 2028 is divisible by 4 and is not a century year, so it is a leap year.
s: States the rule: divisible by 4, but century years only if divisible by 400

questions.q: Under the rule "add one extra day every fourth year": (a) How many days are there in 8 calendar years? (b) How many days does the Earth take for 8 revolutions around the Sun? (c) By how many days is the calendar ahead of the Earth after these 8 years?
Assertion (A): The year 2000 was a leap year. Reason (R): 2000 is divisible by 400.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: 2000 is a century year, and a century year is a leap year only when it is divisible by 400, which 2000 is.

questions.q: Consider the following statements. Statement I: The year 1900 was not a leap year. Statement II: With the rule "an extra day every fourth year, but not in the 100th year", 100 calendar years have 24 leap years. Statement III: With the final leap-year rule, 1000 calendar years have 3,65,240 days. Which of the statements are true?
questions.a: Only I and II: 1900 is a century year not divisible by 400, and 25 - 1 = 24 leap years remain in 100 years. Statement III is false: the final rule gives 3,65,242 days; 3,65,240 was the count before every 400th year was made a leap year.

questions.q: True or False: After 60 calendar years of 365 days each, the Earth still needs 1.4532 more days to complete its 60th revolution around the Sun.
questions.a: False. Each year is 0.2422 day short, so after 60 years the shortfall is 0.2422 × 60 = 14.532 days, not 1.4532 days.

questions.q: A calendar slowly drifts away from the Earth's 365.2422 days per revolution. Rule A adds a leap day in every fourth year with no exceptions. Rule C adds a leap day every fourth year but never in a 100th year. Today's rule is Rule C, plus a leap day in every 400th year. (a) Under Rule A, by how much is the calendar ahead after 100 years? After how many whole centuries is it first at least one full day ahead? (b) Under Rule C, by how much is the calendar behind after 100 years? After how many whole centuries is it first at least one full day behind? (c) Under today's rule there are 97 leap years in 400 years. By how much is the calendar ahead after 400 years, and after how many blocks of 400 years is it first at least one full day ahead? (d) Arrange the three rules from the one that drifts a full day soonest to the one that drifts latest.
questions.a: (a) 100 × 365 + 25 = 36525 days against 100 × 365.2422 = 36524.22, so 0.78 day ahead; after 2 centuries it is 1.56 days ahead (after 1 it is only 0.78), so 2 centuries = 200 years. (b) 36524 against 36524.22, so 0.22 day behind; 4 centuries give 0.88 and 5 give 1.10, so 5 centuries = 500 years. (c) 400 × 365 + 97 = 146097 against 400 × 365.2422 = 146096.88, so 0.12 day ahead; 8 blocks give 0.96 and 9 give 1.08, so 9 blocks = 3600 years. (d) Rule A (200 years), then Rule C (500 years), then today's rule (3600 years).
s: Part (d): A, then C, then today's rule

questions.q: A school in Kanpur always holds its Annual Day on the last day of February. The school office uses the leap-year rule: a year divisible by 4 is a leap year and has 366 days, with February getting a 29th day, except a century year, which is a leap year only if it is divisible by 400. The office is now printing diaries for the years 2027 and 2028. (a) Is 2027 a leap year? On which date is Annual Day in 2027? (b) Is 2028 a leap year? On which date is Annual Day in 2028? (c) How many days does the 2028 diary need for the whole year? (d) The office also finds an old diary from the year 2000. Was 2000 a leap year? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) No, 2027 is not divisible by 4, so Annual Day is on 28 February 2027. (b) Yes, 2028 is divisible by 4 and is not a century year, so Annual Day is on 29 February 2028. (c) 366 days. (d) Yes: 2000 is a century year, but it is divisible by 400.
s: Part (a): not a leap year; 28 February
